title: Tibetan Yoga: Somatic Practice in Vajrayāna Buddhism and Dzogchen (chapter 8 of Yoga in Transformation), section 6 'Tögal: Yoga of Active Perception'
author: Ian A. Baker (quoting Dudjom Lingpa, Jigme Lingpa, Pema Lingpa, Padmasambhava/Khandro Nyingthik, and the Seventeen Tantras)

summary: A scholar-practitioner's chapter on Tibetan somatic yoga whose sixth section describes Tögal as an inversion of sense withdrawal: perception is extended outward into self-manifesting visions said to rest initially on entoptic phenomena. It gives concrete detail drawn from primary texts: the three postures (lion, elephant, sage) with body placement, the gaze paired with each (rolled upward, sideways soft-focus, lowered through half-closed eyes), slow exhalation through slightly parted lips, and 'three-fold motionlessness of body, eyes and consciousness'. It quotes Dudjom Lingpa on how the first lights look (fine moving gold-sheened strands, then strung pearls, then lattices) and Pema Lingpa's point that the visions appear only while the posture is held. Lists the four lamps and four visions. The author explicitly relates the early visions to floaters and blood cells in retinal capillaries.
why_relevant: Openly licensed text carrying specific posture, gaze and breath instructions for open-eye light visions, with quoted primary descriptions of the first appearances; a readable stand-in for in-copyright primary translations.

notes: Academic-press chapter used as a conduit, not as a study. Saved file is the Baker chapter only (OCR; diacritics garbled, e.g. 'Tógal'). Baker cites Dowman 2014 = Dowman's translation of Jigme Lingpa's Yeshe Lama, a text traditionally restricted to those with transmission; the chapter itself is openly published. Footnote 101 mentions a datura decoction applied to the eyes in early texts: plant-induced, logged in excluded_leads.md. The claim that Namkhai Norbu and Thinley Norbu gave details comes as 'personal communication' footnotes (107, 108).
